templates.pattern: A spherical cell has a radius of [R] μm. Calculate the volume of the cell in μm³.
templates.explanation:
Volume of sphere = (4/3)πr³
= (4/3) × π × [R]³
= 4 × 3.14159 × [R*R*R] ÷ 3
= [RESULT] μm³

Volume grows much faster than surface area as radius increases. Doubling the radius increases volume 8-fold but surface area only 4-fold — this is why cells divide rather than grow indefinitely.

templates.pattern: A spherical cell has a radius of [R] μm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cell in μm⁻¹.
templates.explanation:
SA:V ratio of sphere = (4πr²) ÷ (4/3)πr³ = 3 ÷ r
= 3 ÷ [R]
= [RESULT] μm⁻¹

As cell radius doubles the SA:V ratio halves. Small cells are more efficient at exchanging substances. This fundamental relationship drives cell division and the evolution of specialised exchange surfaces.

templates.pattern: Mitosis in a cell type takes [MIT_T] minutes. A sample of cells has a mitotic index of [MI]%. Calculate the total cell cycle length in minutes.
templates.explanation:
Cell cycle length = mitosis duration × 100 ÷ mitotic index
= [MIT_T] × 100 ÷ [MI]
= [RESULT] minutes

This assumes cells are equally likely to be at any stage of the cycle. The mitotic index reflects the proportion of time spent in mitosis relative to the whole cycle.

templates.pattern: A membrane has a surface area of [SA] μm², a concentration difference of [CD] mmol/L, a permeability coefficient of [PERM] and a thickness of [T] μm. Calculate the rate of diffusion in arbitrary units.
templates.explanation:
Extended Fick's Law: rate = (SA × CD × permeability) ÷ thickness
= ([SA] × [CD] × [PERM]) ÷ [T]
= [SA*CD*PERM] ÷ [T]
= [RESULT]

Permeability varies for different molecules. Lipid-soluble molecules cross membranes faster than polar molecules. This is why cell membranes are selectively permeable.

templates.pattern: A DNA molecule undergoes [N] rounds of replication. Calculate the number of new DNA strands produced (excluding the original two strands).
templates.explanation:
New DNA strands = 2ⁿ − 2
= 2^[N] − 2
= [pow(2,N)] − 2
= [RESULT]

Semi-conservative replication produces 2ⁿ total DNA molecules after n rounds. Subtracting 2 gives the number of new molecules since the two original strands are always retained.

templates.pattern: A plant grows from an initial dry mass of [W1] g to a final dry mass of [W2] g over [TIME] days. Calculate the relative growth rate in per day.
templates.explanation:
Relative growth rate = ln(W₂/W₁) ÷ time
= ln([W2]/[W1]) ÷ [TIME]
= ln([MULT]) ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] per day

RGR measures growth relative to existing mass. It allows fair comparison between plants of different sizes. A high RGR means rapid proportional growth.

templates.pattern: An organism has a maximum oxygen uptake (VO₂ max) of [VO2] mL O₂/kg/min and a body mass of [MASS] kg. Calculate the maximum oxygen consumption rate in mL/min.
templates.explanation:
O₂ consumption = VO₂ max × body mass
= [VO2] × [MASS]
= [RESULT] mL/min

VO₂ max is a key measure of aerobic fitness. Elite endurance athletes can have VO₂ max values above 70 mL/kg/min. Untrained individuals are typically 35-45 mL/kg/min.

templates.pattern: An enzyme converts [PRODUCT] nmol of substrate into product in [TIME] seconds. Calculate the enzyme activity in nmol/s.
templates.explanation:
Enzyme activity = product formed ÷ time
= [PRODUCT] ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] nmol/s

Enzyme activity is measured by how much product is formed per unit time. It depends on enzyme concentration, substrate concentration, temperature and pH.

templates.pattern: An enzyme has a reaction rate of [R1] nmol/s at [T1]°C and [R2] nmol/s at [T2]°C where T2 = T1 + 10. Calculate the Q10 temperature coefficient.
templates.explanation:
Q10 = rate at (T+10°C) ÷ rate at T°C
= [R2] ÷ [R1]
= [RESULT]

For most enzymes Q10 ≈ 2 meaning the reaction rate doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature. Above the optimum temperature the rate falls as the enzyme denatures.

templates.pattern: An enzyme has a normal activity of [NORM] nmol/s. In the presence of an inhibitor the activity falls to [INH] nmol/s. Calculate the percentage inhibition.
templates.explanation:
Percentage inhibition = (normal − inhibited) ÷ normal × 100
= ([NORM] − [INH]) ÷ [NORM] × 100
= [RESULT]%

Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the active site shape. Both reduce enzyme activity.
